advisory.checklist_item: - [ ] Extend test_rule_removal_is_detected (or add per-group removal proofs) to demonstrate the LINUX/CAPABILITY/FALLBACK/HOSTILE literal groups also go RED when their block is stripped, and avoid over-generic single-token literals like 'bwrap'.
evidence: LINUX_LITERALS includes the bare token 'bwrap' (line 47) which appears elsewhere in the block (e.g. the capability-probe prose) and could remain even if the Linux code fence were removed.
No test asserts the literals appear *inside a fenced code block* or in the intended section, only that the substring exists anywhere in the file.
advisory.finding: The regression gate's self-check (test_rule_removal_is_detected) proves sensitivity only for the MACOS_LITERALS group by stripping a single literal; the LINUX_LITERALS, CAPABILITY_LITERALS, FALLBACK_LITERALS, and HOSTILE_CODE_LITERALS groups have no equivalent removal proof. Several of those literals are generic single tokens ('bwrap', 'injected seam', 'arbitrary code') that could survive an otherwise gutted block, weakening the gate for those parts.
scenarios: A future edit removes the Linux code fence but leaves prose mentioning 'bwrap'; test_skill_carries_complete_linux_invocation may still pass on the surviving fragments.
The self-guard gives false confidence that all literal groups are removal-sensitive when only one is proven.

advisory.checklist_item: - [ ] Narrow test_skill_frames_the_mutation_as_hostile_code to the security-relevant tokens (e.g. that a hostile-code framing and a sandbox rationale exist) rather than exact narrative phrasings ('hostile code' vs 'arbitrary code', the literal date, '/opt/homebrew'), which break on a behavior-preserving reword.
evidence: Rubric: 'An LLM is NOT a non-human consumer — a prose/heading grep that merely guards the author's wording IS a change-detector.'

The operational contract (that the mutation run is sandboxed) is fully carried by the macOS/Linux command literals; requiring both 'arbitrary code' AND 'hostile code' and the exact incident date tests wording, not the sandbox behavior.
advisory.finding: test_skill_frames_the_mutation_as_hostile_code is a change-detector: it asserts prose-narrative literals ('arbitrary code', 'hostile code', '2026-08-26', 'rm -rf /*', '/opt/homebrew') whose only consumer is a human reader of the rationale. A behavior-preserving reword of the incident narrative (different date, 'attacker-controlled' vs 'hostile', a differently phrased example) breaks the test while the actual security requirement — the sandbox invocation — is unchanged. Per Rule 4, this breaks on a reword with no observable-behavior change.

blocking.checklist_item: - [ ] Add a writable scratch bind to the Linux bwrap invocation (e.g. `--bind "$SBX" "$SBX"` with SBX=$(mktemp -d), matching the macOS profile) so it honors the 'worktree and a scratch dir' contract.
evidence: SKILL.md:807: 'inside an OS sandbox that denies writes outside the worktree and a scratch dir.'
macOS profile (SKILL.md:818-819) allows both `(subpath "$PWD")` and `(subpath "$SBX")`, but the Linux argv binds only $PWD writable — no scratch dir equivalent.
Ticket verification only checked 'the write inside the bind succeeded and a write outside failed' — it did not verify a test command needing a writable temp dir succeeds.
blocking.finding: The prescribed Linux `bwrap` invocation provides no writable scratch directory, contradicting the block's own stated contract ('an OS sandbox that denies writes outside the worktree and a scratch dir') and diverging from the macOS profile, which allows writes to both $PWD and the scratch dir $SBX. `--ro-bind / /` mounts everything read-only except $PWD, /dev, /proc, so a mutation test command that writes to /tmp or $TMPDIR (e.g. pytest tmp_path, temp build artifacts) fails with 'Read-only file system'.
scenarios: An agent on Linux runs a pytest-based mutation check that writes to tmp_path / $TMPDIR under the sandbox; the run fails on 'Read-only file system' rather than exercising the mutation.
Operator follows the copy-paste Linux snippet expecting parity with the documented macOS behaviour.
blocking.suggested_fix: Prepend `SBX="$(mktemp -d)"` and add `--bind "$SBX" "$SBX"` (and optionally `--setenv TMPDIR "$SBX"`) to the bwrap argv so the Linux sandbox offers the same writable scratch dir the macOS profile does.

dropped.checklist_item: - [ ] Make the bwrap capability probe surface its failure via exit status (e.g. `if ! bwrap --ro-bind / / -- /bin/true; then echo 'bwrap cannot namespace here' >&2; exit 1; fi`) so a caller can gate on it rather than swallowing the failure with `|| echo`.
evidence: The `|| echo ...` swallows the non-zero status; the pipeline's final exit code is 0 whether or not bwrap can namespace.

Litmus: in the world where bwrap 'is present but cannot namespace' (Ubuntu 23.10+ AppArmor, cited in the same block), the probe still exits 0 — the failure is only a visible-if-a-human-reads-it string, not a status a caller can gate on.
dropped.finding: The bwrap capability probe is presented as the gate for whether a sandbox exists, but its failure signal fails open: `bwrap --ro-bind / / -- /bin/true || echo "bwrap cannot namespace here"` only prints a message on failure and the whole expression exits 0, so any wrapper or agent keying off the probe's exit status cannot distinguish 'bwrap works' from 'bwrap cannot namespace'. The negative verdict is indistinguishable from success.
scenarios: A follow-on wrapper (the ticket notes scripts/mutation_sandbox.py is planned) shells out to this probe and branches on returncode — it always sees success and proceeds unsandboxed.
An agent scripts the probe and keys on exit code rather than stdout text.
dropped.suggested_fix: Replace `bwrap ... -- /bin/true || echo "..."` with a form that preserves a non-zero exit on probe failure so downstream automation cannot treat 'cannot namespace' as success.
